chapter: Reel IV retellings and New York pianists
title: Ethel Waters at the Lafayette, Earl Dancer and the union
summary: He made orchestrations for Ethel Waters, producer Earl Dancer ran off with the money, and Whaley took the manager to the union and was kept out of the theatre for a year.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Now I don't want to interrupt you because it's your story, but you were telling me about Lucky Roberts. When did you run in to Claude Hopkins?
I didn't run into Claude until after -- Claude was playing down at the Roseland, and this was in '28, and I got the job at the theatre, see, and I got a band and went into the Lafayette Theatre.

And Ethel Waters was the star, and she didn't have any music, and I said, well, you got to have some orchestration -- and she said, 'My piano player will tell them what to play.' So finally, I made some orchestrations for her.
Who was her pianist?
It wasn't Reginald Beame, but who was the girl -- what was the girl's name? Ruby.
Oh? I didn't know here.
Yeah. Ruby was a piano player.
Oh, she had a girl piano player.
Yeah, at first, and then she got
Reginald Beame.
Uh huh.
And I played there ...
Face this way, Tom.
So I played that way until Earl Dancer came in there.
Who was Earl Dancer?
Earl Dancer, he was a playboy around town then.
He married her -- he was one of her many husbands, huh?
Yeah, and he run off -- he collected all the money but $55, that was for the chorus girls and the band.
It wouldn't be like a high class pimp, would he?

Yeah, just like one. And I took Shipman down to the union, and Shipman was ordered to pay all the musicians, so Shipman fired me out of a' job, see. And I used to hang around the theatre there, and one day I caught Shipman out on the side, and I said, 'You act like a kid, when a kid hits you, the kid cries, and you're doing that to me -- I couldn't pay them guys, them guys are looking for the money, and you're letting the man run off with all the money. And just because I took you down to the union, you fired me out of a job.'
So after awhile, let me see, he kept me out of the theatre for nearly a year ...
